title: Who Keeps The Plate
concept: A brand new plate-reading camera with a face is sawn off its pole in an Anchorage lot, and the film asks who decides what it keeps. The October 20th vote governs the city's own cameras, not the store's pole, so the pole answers to a retailer and a vendor. The film ends on three questions to put to any automated camera.

fingerprint.palette: Anchorage night slate, pale drifts, charcoal asphalt, sodium amber for the store, magenta for the vendor, civic blue for the city, cyan for the machine reading
fingerprint.metaphor: a camera's receipt tape of what it saw, and three coloured rulebooks (store, vendor, city) fighting over who may cut it

palette: Anchorage night slate, pale drifts, charcoal asphalt, sodium amber for the store, magenta for the vendor, civic blue for the city, cyan for the machine reading
divergence_note: 10-09 was a dusk utility yard with a steel tank and a power gauge, 10-08 a dawn pier with a burning glass lens. This film is a night parking lot under sodium lamps with a pole camera that has one big eye, plus a newsroom desk, a civic hall, a plan-view boundary, a wall of 750 sockets and a document desk. The look is colour-coded by who owns a rule (amber store, magenta vendor, civic blue city, cyan machine), where 10-09 coded electricity and the model. The hero is a street-level machine that can be sawn off its pole, and the argument is carried by cutting between many worlds, where 10-09 held one yard.

angle.thesis: The camera someone cut down belongs to a store and the October 20th vote governs the city's own cameras, so Anchorage is arguing about the visible pole while the rules that matter sit with a retailer, a vendor and the city, and the honest questions to ask of any automated camera are what it keeps, for how long and who gets it.
angle.falsifier: If either proposed ordinance (AO 2026-108 or the mayor's 108(S)) reaches the data a private business collects, or if the news and the ordinances already describe what the software extracts, the thesis is false. The facts set shows the ordinances cover city surveillance data, and the vendor's own FAQ is the only source that says machine learning and vehicle traits.
supporting_facts: f1 Flock began installing plate readers for an unnamed private customer, cameras went up at Anchorage Lowe's stores
f6 Lowe's keeps such data typically no more than 90 days and shares with service providers and NCMEC, Flock's own FAQ default is 7 days
f7 APD doesn't use Flock and has no feed, but its own readers ride in patrol cars under an Axon contract
f8 the two proposed ordinances split on retention, outside networks and Assembly approval of purchases
f11 Flock's own FAQ says the cameras apply machine learning and capture make, color and body type, no news article calls it AI
angle.counterpoint: The mayor says the Assembly version could unduly limit core APD functions, a store may put a camera on its own pole, Lowe's publishes a ceiling, and a customer's privacy statement may be rule enough. The fair case gets a full scene at full strength. And the residents who reject the capability outright aren't answered by rules about who controls it.
runner_ups: Pure who-holds-the-data structure story (analyst 2): folded in as the three rulebooks spine.
Pro-capability governance frame (analyst 1): its counter-case became the Test scene.
Honest-AI machine vision (analyst 3): supplies the cutaway of what the machine reads and the three questions button.
angle.second_movement: The cameras people are fighting over aren't the biggest system in town. The city's own Axon deal is $11.8 million over five years for up to 750 camera feeds, plate readers and drones, and that is what the vote governs.

treatment.winner: The Dramatist's structure (the saw cold open, the Test, three rulebooks) with the Comedian's NEW! ribbon and rolling shopping cart, the Explainer's receipt TAPE as the throughline and the make, color, body type tags, and the Enthusiast's honest wonder at what the machine reads
treatment.why: All four pitches converged on a faced pole camera and the three questions button. The Dramatist drew the fair counter-case as a named scene, the Explainer's tape gave the 7 versus 90 day comparison a physical form, and the ordinance check confirmed the structural reveal that both proposed rules bind only the city. The storyboard critic's revision moved Flock's statements to a neutral newsroom desk so the film never implies the customer is Lowe's.

shots.title: The pole they cut
shots.means: Hook. A brand new PoleCam with a NEW! ribbon blinks awake on its pole in a snowy night lot while an installer's ladder slides away and a pickup rolls through, its tape printing a tiny truck. A saw blade's tip and shadow wait at frame left from the first frame, then it strokes the pole, which topples into the snow with a puff. The lens goes dark beside a pure scribble hand sign.
